The layoff email reached Noor's inbox on a Monday, and by Wednesday Noor could explain it perfectly. Over chai at the stall outside their Bengaluru office, in her last week there, she told Hafsa about market corrections, cost-per-employee ratios and why the design team was an obvious cut. "It's not personal. Honestly, it's logical."
Hafsa, who had mentored her for two years, listened. She also noticed the untouched bun-maska, the dark circles, the 2:47 a.m. time on Noor's last message about "restructuring trends".
When Noor paused, Hafsa didn't ask about the market. "Leave the logic for a minute. How are you, really?"
Noor opened her mouth to answer with a number, then didn't. She stared into her chai. "Scared," she said finally. "And kind of ashamed."
Hafsa pulled her stool a little closer and waited.

qa.a: Explaining it keeps it impersonal and under control, so she doesn't have to feel the fear and shame of losing the job.

qa.q: Which choice of Hafsa's opened the conversation up?
qa.a: Setting the logic aside and asking how Noor really was, which let the truth come out: 'Scared' and 'kind of ashamed'.

qa.q: What might it have meant to Noor that Hafsa asked about her rather than the market?
qa.a: Noor may have felt seen for the first time since Monday, allowed to be scared instead of having to sound logical.

I've managed people for only three years, so I almost missed it. When Joseph was laid off from our team in March, he handled it better than I did. He wrote a clear handover document. He told me, "It's a budget decision, not a performance one. I understand the reasoning." He even helped me draft the announcement to the team. But I began noticing his lunch box going home full, and his status blinking online past two in the morning. His calm seemed too complete.
On his last Thursday, I took him for a walk around the lake behind our office. Instead of asking about his next steps, I asked, "How does it actually feel?" He walked for a while. Then he said, "Like I did everything right and it didn't matter." I didn't try to fix it. I just said I was glad he'd told me. Looking back, I, Anjali, nearly praised his calm instead of asking.

qa.q: What did Joseph help Anjali draft?
qa.a: The announcement to the team.

qa.q: What did Joseph's line 'I did everything right and it didn't matter' suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: Hurt and powerless, as if his effort had been wasted; the neat handover had been holding that feeling down.

qa.q: Which choice on the last Thursday made the difference?
qa.a: Taking him for a walk and asking how it felt rather than about next steps, then listening without trying to fix it.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team have read Joseph's calm?
qa.a: They may have admired how well he handled it and never noticed the full lunch box or the late nights.

grounding: A manager notices that a laid-off team member's reasonable calm comes with skipped lunches and late nights, and asks how it feels rather than what comes next.

Mentor's notes, Sunaina, Thursday
Aniket, from my old team, was laid off in the restructuring two weeks ago. We still meet every Thursday.
Today he walked me through it like a case study: "Revenue dipped eight percent, they cut the newest hires in two units, it's statistically sensible." Clear, calm, well argued.
What I noticed: he hasn't eaten at our last three meetings; he orders black coffee and leaves the sandwich. He mentioned he'd "optimised" his sleep to five hours so he could apply for more roles. His laptop stayed open the whole time, thirty-one tabs.
What I did: I closed my own notebook and asked, "Not what it means. How does it feel?" He began explaining the market again, stopped, and said, "Like I got thrown out." We sat with that. I bought him a proper lunch and he ate half.
Next: meet again Monday, not Thursday.

qa.q: What does Aniket order at their meetings instead of eating?
qa.a: Black coffee, leaving the sandwich.

qa.q: Why might explaining the layoff like a case study feel reasonable to Aniket?
qa.a: Treating it as numbers makes it impersonal and manageable, so he doesn't have to feel the sting of being let go; the skipped meals hint that the calm is thinner than it sounds.

qa.q: What turning point came from Sunaina's question?
qa.a: Asking how it felt rather than what it meant let Aniket drop the market explanation and say "Like I got thrown out", which opened the real conversation.

qa.q: Why might Sunaina move the next meeting up to Monday?
qa.a: Sunaina has seen the skipped meals and short sleep behind the calm and likely wants to check in sooner, showing care without pushing.

Sat, 11 pm
Met Gopika for chai at the old press club canteen, first time since the paper shut the features desk. She was so composed. She talked about ad revenue, falling print numbers, how "any rational editor" would have cut features first. She even drew me a little graph on a napkin.
But her eyes had dark rings, she admitted she'd been up till four most nights "reading industry reports", and she said she'd mostly been living on tea. Her samosa went cold on the plate.
I almost argued with the graph. Instead I said, "That all makes sense. But how does it feel, Gopika?" She folded the napkin into smaller and smaller squares. Then: "Like all those years of wanting this job just... vanished." Her voice cracked. We stayed till the canteen closed.
I'll call her Tuesday. Just to check in.
Sangeeta

qa.q: What did Gopika draw on a napkin?
qa.a: A little graph.

qa.q: What does Gopika folding the napkin into smaller squares suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the composed explanation was holding back strong feelings, and that as the question landed she was struggling with them before she could speak.

qa.q: Which choice by Sangeeta opened up the conversation?
qa.a: Not arguing with the graph but agreeing it made sense and then asking how it felt, which let Gopika move from reasons to the loss itself.

qa.q: What might the evening have meant for Gopika by the time the canteen closed?
qa.a: Gopika may have felt lighter and less alone for having said it aloud, even though the sadness about the job was still there.

grounding: Illustrates a mentor who sees a junior explain losing her job in calm, rational terms while skipping sleep and meals, and asks about the feeling instead of the meaning.
